keyVerseText: And Abram said, Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?
rootMeaning: The word יְהֹוִה (Yᵉhôvih) is a variation of the divine name יְהֹוָה (Yᵉhôvâh), which is rooted in the concept of 'the existing One.' This name emphasizes God's eternal, self-existent nature, distinguishing Him as the one true God. The variation יְהֹוִה arises from a linguistic practice to avoid repeating the same vowel sounds, often used after the title אֲדֹנָי and pronounced as אֱלֹהִים. This subtle shift in pronunciation and formality reflects reverence and the sacredness of God's personal name beyond the common English term 'God.'
usageInScripture: The term יְהֹוִה appears approximately 250 times in the Hebrew Scriptures, predominantly translated simply as 'GOD' in 247 instances. This consistent translation underscores the recognition of this name as the proper designation for the divine being. A few occurrences translate the term in more specific phrases such as 'and unto GOD,' 'thou for me O GOD,' and 'O GOD,' showing occasional contextual nuances but always pointing to the sovereign deity. The frequent use and translation highlight the centrality of this name in the biblical text as the personal and covenantal name of God.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding the original meaning of יְהֹוִה enriches our grasp of God's self-existence and eternal nature, foundational truths for Christian faith. This divine name reveals God not as a distant force but as the living, sustaining One who is always present. Recognizing יְהֹוִה as the personal name of God invites believers into a relationship with Him that is intimate and reverent. It also affirms the continuity of God's revelation from the Old Testament to the New, where Jesus Christ embodies the fullness of this eternal God. Thus, this name anchors our faith in the unchanging and faithful character of God revealed throughout Scripture.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 15:2, Abram addresses God as 'Lord GOD,' using the divine name יְהֹוִה to express his direct appeal to the covenantal and sovereign God. This usage highlights Abram's recognition of God's authority and faithfulness even in moments of personal uncertainty. The presence of this name in the verse emphasizes God's role as the active, living Lord who hears and responds to His people's concerns, reinforcing the intimate and trustworthy nature of God revealed through His name.
